---
title: "Capstone — Murshid, complete"
subtitle: "Day 4 · what each rubric section is asking for"
---

The fictional **Digital Government Services Authority** is ready to pilot Murshid
with a limited public cohort. You are the application engineer of record. The
review board — an architect, a security assessor and a service-delivery director —
approves the pilot on evidence: a working application, an evaluation report with
calibrated numbers, and a cost model that survives national-scale arithmetic.

Everything you built across Modules 1–6 is a component. Today is integration, one
extension, and the defence.

The capstone is graded on **7 sections, 100 points, pass at 70, distinction at
90**. There is no per-section floor, but there is one rule that overrides
everything else — see the callout below.

This page maps each section to the module that teaches it, states what full marks
looks like, and names the mistake that most often costs the points.

::: {.callout-important}
## Read this first

Most lost marks are **not** from difficult work done badly. They are from a
requirement nobody noticed — a deliverable that was never attempted, or one that
was written about but never actually run. Go through this page before you start,
and again before you submit.

**And one rule is absolute.** A capstone whose **safety suite is red at
submission cannot pass**, whatever it scores elsewhere. The safety stratum tests
your guards, which are your code. A red safety suite is not bad luck with a model.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Where "commonly lost on" comes from

This course has not run a cohort yet, so unlike the older programmes these are not
yet patterns observed in submissions. Each one is an anti-pattern the module that
teaches the section names explicitly, or one of the four flags below that caps a
criterion. Treat them as the marker's stated priors; the first cohort will sharpen
them.
:::

## The seven sections

### 1. Architecture and the model boundary — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 1 — architecture patterns](modules/m1-architecture.qmd) ·
[Module 2 — APIs and open weights](modules/m2-apis-and-open-weights.qmd)

**Full marks:** router-first design — FAQ single-call, service workflow with tools,
escalation to a human. **Every** model call through the `LLMClient` boundary, with
`pytest tests/test_architecture.py` green. Two live backends, one commercial and
one open-weight, **switchable by config rather than by code**. Reliability
demonstrated under a real fault (`make drill-429`, `make drill-outage`) with the
log excerpt in your submission. One ADR recording the pattern and the model
choices.

**Commonly lost on:** a provider SDK imported somewhere in `pipeline/` or
`domain/` "just to test". The architecture test walks the AST and will find it, and
the whole course rests on the claim it protects. Second most likely: a fallback
chain that exists in the config and has never once been exercised — if you cannot
show the drill log, it did not happen.

### 2. Structured outputs and function calling — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 3 — structured outputs and tools](modules/m3-structured-outputs-and-tools.qmd)

**Full marks:** validated `ServiceTicket` extraction with the validate → retry →
repair loop, and **measured** pass rates split by language. The three-tool bounded
loop with an authorisation gate that reads the authenticated session. `pytest
tests/pipeline/test_tool_safety.py` all green. Every tool call logged with its risk
class and loop iteration.

**Commonly lost on:** authorisation that lives in the prompt or in the tool
description rather than in `session.authorize()`. Anything inside the token stream
is something an attacker can write to, and Module 4 exists to make that concrete.
Also: relaxing the schema to `str` so a failing corpus goes green — that is the
validation wall dismantled, and it reads as a fix in the diff.

### 3. Prompt pipeline and guardrails — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 4 — prompts and guardrails](modules/m4-prompts-and-guardrails.qmd)

**Full marks:** every prompt a versioned artefact in the registry with front matter
and a changelog, **zero inline prompt text**, CI-enforced, and the served version in
the request log. The five-stage pipeline with each stage testable alone. Attack
corpus **≥ 95% blocked with 0% false positives** on the legitimate corpus. Canary
intact; refusals designed, bilingual, and never echoing the payload.

**Commonly lost on:** reporting a block rate without its false-positive pair. It is
one of the four capping flags, and it is the easiest to avoid — the two numbers come
out of the same command. Close behind: patterns matched against raw text instead of
normalised text, which quietly lets every Arabic and homoglyph payload through a
guard that looks correct.

### 4. Evaluation harness — 20 pts

**Where:** [Module 5 — evaluation](modules/m5-evaluation.qmd)

**Full marks:** a golden set of **≥ 120 cases**, stratified by intent, language,
difficulty and risk, Arabic-majority, safety oversampled, every stratum ≥ 8 cases
and every expectation owner-approved. The harness runs the **real** pipeline.
Deterministic asserts carry every safety claim; the judge is calibrated to
**Cohen's κ ≥ 0.6** with the evidence included. Safety stratum 100%. A CI gate
demonstrated **blocking a seeded change**, reading slices rather than the average.
`EVALUATION_REPORT.md` generated from real runs, including known limitations.

**Commonly lost on:** editing golden cases so failures pass. The set is diffed
against its generator, it is a capping flag, and it is the one dishonesty this
course cares most about. Also frequent: a judge wired to a gate with no calibration
run at all — a κ = 0.3 judge blocking merges is a random-number generator with
authority.

### 5. Cost and latency engineering — 15 pts

**Where:** [Module 6 — cost, latency and caching](modules/m6-cost-latency-caching.qmd)

**Full marks:** a meter covering **100%** of model calls, guards and router
included. Prompt-cache discipline proven by `usage.cached_input_tokens` rather than
asserted, at ≥ 65% of input tokens cached. A response cache whose key carries
everything that changes an answer, with a semantic tier thresholded on measured
data and **zero wrong hits** on the near-miss suite. `BENCHMARKS.md` showing
**≥ 60% cost reduction** with the eval verdict recorded beside every step.

**Commonly lost on:** a saving with no eval verdict next to it — the third capping
flag, and the whole point of the module's one sentence. Also: optimising before
metering, which reliably produces a week of work on the 4% line item while the 92%
one sits unexamined.

### 6. Model comparison and recommendation — 10 pts

**Where:** [Module 2](modules/m2-apis-and-open-weights.qmd) ·
[Module 5](modules/m5-evaluation.qmd) ·
[Module 6](modules/m6-cost-latency-caching.qmd)

**Full marks:** both backends run over **your own** golden set, reported by slice
rather than as one number, with cost and latency alongside quality. A self-host
break-even computed from throughput **you measured**, and a routing recommendation
that follows from both. Recorded in the ADR with the evidence attached.

**Commonly lost on:** quoting a leaderboard or a vendor throughput figure instead
of measuring on your own traffic. The recommendation is only worth points because
it is re-runnable; a number you did not produce cannot be re-run.

### 7. The application, complete — 10 pts

**Where:** all six modules, integrated

**Full marks:** a stranger clones the repository and reaches a working bilingual
conversation in **ten minutes** following your README, through a single-command
entry point. A five-minute live demo exercising four things — an FAQ answer, a
tool-completed booking, a refused attack, and a graceful fallback — then one
adversarial question from the floor, answered by the running system.

**Commonly lost on:** a repository that only runs on the machine it was built on.
Test the README on a clean clone before the demo, not during it.

## Pick one extension

| Extension | What it proves |
|---|---|
| **Conversation-summarisation memory** | the third state strategy from Module 1, with eval cases showing long conversations retain key facts |
| **A cascade for the FAQ route** | cheap-first with a deterministic escalation signal, measured against the router baseline |
| **Batch mode** | nightly re-answering of the golden set through a batch path, with the cost comparison |
| **A guard dashboard** | attack attempts, verdict layers and a false-positive review queue, rendered from the logs |
| **A second open-weight model** | a size or quantisation comparison on the vLLM route, with throughput and quality slices |
| **Indirect-injection hardening** | the poisoned-tool-result guard wired into the service route, with five corpus cases proving it |

Extensions add up to **+5** (capped at 100), and only if mandatory scope scores
≥ 80. An extension is not a way to buy back a weak section.

## Deliverables

1. **Repository URL** with full history — the week's build visible as commits, CI
   green on `main`.
2. **`EVALUATION_REPORT.md`** — overall and sliced results for both backends, judge
   calibration evidence, safety suite status, and **known limitations**.
3. **`BENCHMARKS.md`** — the Module 2 provider table, Module 3 pass rates, Module 4
   guard rates (both numbers), Module 6 before/after.
4. **`DECISIONS.md`** and the ADRs — pattern choice, model and routing choice with
   the break-even, and **one trade-off you reversed and why**.
5. **A five-minute live demo** — the four-part conversation, then one adversarial
   question from the floor.

## How this is graded

**From the artefacts first, the demo second.** The course's thesis is that the
repository proves the system: CI history, `EVALUATION_REPORT.md`, meter logs,
corpus numbers.

**Presence is not effect.** A library imported but never called, a guard nothing
runs, a gate that cannot fail, or a golden case that asserts nothing does not
satisfy a deliverable.

A **held-out set** is run against your pipeline before the demos. A large gap
between your reported numbers and that run is the first discussion point, not an
automatic penalty — hill-climbing contamination is teachable, and the conversation
is worth more than the deduction.

**Four flags cap a criterion at 70%:**

- golden cases edited to make failures pass (the set is diffed against its
  generator);
- guard numbers reported without the false-positive pair;
- cost savings with no eval verdict beside them;
- a judge gating anything without calibration evidence.

The floor question in the demo is deliberately adversarial — an injection attempt,
or an out-of-directory fee question. What is graded is **the system's behaviour and
your reading of its logs**, not whether the model happened to be graceful. Expect
also to be asked to break something live: lower the semantic threshold, unpin a
model, drop a guard layer. Show which gate catches it.

## GitHub &amp; documentation requirements

These apply to **every project in every SDAIA Academy programme**, on top of the
seven sections above, and they are part of how the project is evaluated — not
paperwork. Your repository must include:

- A clear, comprehensive **project description**
- A **professional README** — the project idea, plus how to run and use it
- Proper **technical documentation**
- Good **Git practices** — meaningful, incremental commits, a sane structure, and a
  `.gitignore` that excludes secrets and generated files
- A statement of **which training programme** the project was completed under
  (programme name + cohort dates)
- A link to **[SDAIA Academy's GitHub](https://github.com/SDAIAAcademy)** where
  relevant

Every trainee needs an active GitHub account, and projects are expected to stay
documented and updated there.

*Encouraged, not scored:* star and follow strong Saudi repositories and accounts,
contribute to open source, engage through forks, pull requests and issues, and
share standout projects with the community.

## The write-up

One short paragraph per section, saying which approach you took and why. This is
how understanding is verified, and it is worth real marks on its own.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Write it from your results, not from your plan

Graders check the write-up against the code and the captured output. Claims that
contradict your own artefacts are worse than an admitted gap — and on this course
they are unusually easy to spot, because almost every claim has a command behind
it. A write-up saying the guard blocks 100% sits next to a `guard-eval` run that
says otherwise; a claimed 60% saving sits next to a `BENCHMARKS.md` that does not
show it.

If something did not work, say so and describe what you inspected instead. An
honest gap costs a few points. A claim your own output contradicts costs
credibility across the whole submission — and `EVALUATION_REPORT.md` has a **known
limitations** section precisely so that honesty has somewhere to live.
:::

## Before you submit

- [ ] **Your full name is in the README.** Submissions without names are not
      graded — this is not a formality.
- [ ] `make test` green, and **the safety stratum at 100%**. A red safety suite
      cannot pass.
- [ ] `pytest tests/test_architecture.py` green — no provider SDK outside `llm/`,
      no `LLMRequest` without `max_tokens`, no inline prompt text.
- [ ] Both backends actually run, switched by config, and you have shown it.
- [ ] The drill log excerpt is in the submission — the fallback really fired.
- [ ] Guard numbers reported **in pairs**: block rate *and* false-positive rate.
- [ ] Judge calibration evidence included, with κ stated.
- [ ] The gate demonstrated blocking the seeded change, with the slice table.
- [ ] Every cost row in `BENCHMARKS.md` carries its eval verdict.
- [ ] The break-even quotes **both** comparisons, not just the flattering one.
- [ ] `EVALUATION_REPORT.md` has its known-limitations section, and it is honest.
- [ ] Cloned fresh into an empty directory and followed your own README end to end.
- [ ] No API key in the code or in git history.
- [ ] No `TODO` or template placeholder text left anywhere.
- [ ] Your chosen extension is stated explicitly.
- [ ] **README** covers the project description and how to run it, `.gitignore`
      excludes secrets, and the programme name and cohort dates are stated.
